Every man in Canada should have only one voice-the same voice for Nova Scotia, British Columbia and North Norfolk. I hope that that hon. gentleman will come to the conclusion that one voice is enough for any public man in this country; and he must use his one voice with great caution, or he will get into such trouble as I fear the hon. gentleman has got into tonight. The point I wish to make against the hon. member for North Norfolk is that he did not treat this House fairly this afternoon. I sat here listening to him, and the impression he left on my mind by reading this paper, and I venture to say on the mind of every other man who heard him, was that Sir Sandford Fleming had generally endorsed this scheme. I undertake to say, after reading this paper, that Sir Sand-ford Fleming has made the most severe and destructive criticism of this measure that has yet been made. If the hon. member for North Norfolk cannot summon any better evidence than this interview, he has a hopeless case. For I have learned that that hon. gentleman is very ingenious in suborning testimony-I do not use the word in an offensive sense; for any hon. gentleman who can read this interview as supporting this scheme, suborns it-pulls it away from truth and right. I agree with Sir Sandford Fleming; I want a railway built; I want two or three transcontinental railways built, only I want to select the best route; and I support the amendment of the hon. member for Bothwell. It does not mean delay. If parliament had been treated with proper respect, we could have had a report on the Table of the House to-day from the men best acquainted with the trade routes of this country. If the government had pursued the intention they originally announced of submitting this question to experts, we could have had a report from these experts to-day, and we would now be considering and settling upon the best route. we ask is that it should be put off for six or nine months, in order that we may realize the best hopes of the people of Canada. Those of us who are from Nova Scotia are deeply interested in the selection of this route. For thirty-five years we have been waiting for the fulfilment of pledges which were given to us in that regard; and the action of this government is to destroy our hopes for the next forty years. And when I hear the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) and other hon. gentlemen from Nova Scotia defending this scheme, I long to see them endorsing and defending it before the people. I for my part declare that I will give no party any support against the interests of my province or against the interests of the maritime provinces. Let us come back to this interview. If Cox would wait, I have no doubt the government could employ Sir Sandford Fleming as a consulting engineer. If they did, I venture to say that he would tell us, your route is all wrong. The selection of the route south of Lake Winnipeg is a most cruel disappointment to the people of Canada. Lake Winnipeg dominates the whole trade routes of Canada, and the sooner we realize that the better. Here we have a lake 200 miles long, running north and south, with only a strip of teritory 65 miles wide between that and the United States border. Are you going to crowd all the trade routes of this continent into that strip of territory? You have already two transcontinental railways there. Do not let any man from the west think that I would deny him a mile of railway. If any other railways are needed to relieve the congestion, let branches be built to the lines already existing. A short railway of 400 or 500 miles would be a trifling thing to relieve the congestion. We are not dealing with that. We are dealing with a great transcontinental railway that ought to determine the future of Canada on this continent for all time, and I ask hon. gentlemen in this parliament, is it not time to forget little party questions in the presence of a great question like this ? It strikes me that the appeals to party made by the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister is rather an insult to their supporters. Their supporters should see that at this time in the history of Canada there should be no party appeals in the settlement of a great question like this, but we should sit down, as the great Council of Canada, and confer together and get all the information possible before deciding. I would rather sit here another three months than come to a premature decision. Let us vote $1,000,000 or $1,500,000 to bring out experts from England, Germany and France, who will go over the country, and let us wait for their report before committing ourselves to a false policy. Sir Sandford Fleming condemns the policy of the government from beginning to end. In condemning the east-

era wing, I think he is unwise, for if this railway is to be built, the eastern wing should be constructed as well as the other, but there is room for differences of opinion. On this side we have our differences, but we are all united in oppositi m to this scheme. We approach your citadel from different roads but will overthrow you in the end. When I introduced this amendment I said Jt was intended merely for the purpose of making superabundantly clear what was already absolutely clear under the contract. In my opinion, no one could construe this contract as meaning that any one could import goods free of duty; hut out of deference to the earnest opinion expressed by lion, gentlemen opposite I introduced this amendment. When my hon. friend talks about extending the operation of this section with respect to

betterments, I cannot quite understand bis object. It be is opposed to the idea of tbe government importing goods free of duty, be is opposed to tbe legislation we have had since 1886. The law we have now is what we have had since 1886 and has never been departed from.

I take the point that the road under lease ceases to he a government road, and is a private road, to all intents and purposes, and is not, therefore, in the same position as the Intercolonial Railway. Under this agreement, the Grand Trunk Railway can force the government to import all its materials for betterment during forty-three years free of duty, and will be only bound to pay interest on the net cost. That would be a most serious blow to our manufacturers. To show the Minister of Justice that his own friends interpret this clause as we do, let me point out that the Toronto ' Star ' takes the position, as a matter of course, that on the original construction the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will not have to pay 3 per cent on the duties collected by the government. The provision cannot therefore be so clear as the hon. minister thinks it is, or the government organ in Ontario would hardly have published an editorial showing that tile contract was so plainly in the opposite direction. If the government refuse to provide protection for the materials to be used in con* nection with the betterment of this road, they will do the manufacturers an injury which cannot be over-estimated.

My hon. friend the Minister of Justice says that the law has been the same since 1886 and that we cannot change it now. Let me quote the law from the remarks delivered -by my hon. friend in this House on the 15th of September. He said :
I do not know whether it would convince anybody or not, but I want to satisfy myself. Section 5 of the Customs Act provides : ,
Subject to the same provisions and to the further conditions contained in schedule B to this Act, all goods enumerated in this schedule B may be imported into Canada or may be taken out of warehouse for consumption in Canada without the payment of any duties of customs the-reon.
Then he goes on to say :
Then article 50 of schedule B reads as follows :
Articles imported by or for the use at the Dominion government, or of any of the departments thereof, or by and for the Senate or House of Commons, including the follow-iug articles when imported by the said government or through any of the departments thereof for the use of the Canadian militia : military clothing, musical instruments for military bands, military stores and munitions of war.
It is plain from that quotation that it was never contemplated, when this section was passed in 1886, that such enormous importations would be made as are contemplated by the present agreement. The enumeration
381J
made in this section shows that. It comprises articles for use in the House of Commons and the Senate, and a special mention is made of what is required for the Militia Department. This shows it was never contemplated, when this section was passed, that such enormous importations would be made as will be necessary to improve the road after it is leased to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. We are face to face with this fact, that in fifteen years, according to railway experts, the capital account of the railway will be double. Therefore, if this road is to cost $100,000,000, you will have importations, within the next fifteen years, which will probably amount to $60,000,000 or $70,000,000. When this section was enacted, which my hon. friend quoted the other day, it could not have been in the contemplation of parliament that such enormous importations would be made free of duty to the detriment of our manufacturers. I understand the argument which my hon. friend put before the House the other day to be that, as to the original cost of construction, as defined in section- 15, there can be no -difficulty ; that on any material imported for the original construction of -the road by contractors acting for the government, under the terms of the agreement between the parties, the customs duties would have to be paid on these importations. So far, so good. But my hou. and l-eamed friend -says that when it comes to the betterments no customs duties are to be paid, because the importations are to -be made directly by the government, and they would fall under section 50 of the Customs Act, which he quoted and which I have just referred to. Whether my hon. friend was right or not in the construction of this section the other day would be a merely academic question to be -discussed, because he has made it dear by this amendment. But what we say is that he does not go far enough. We say that mot only should customs duties be paid on materials used in the construction of the road through contractors, but on the immense importations that will be made for improvements, and betterments duties should be paid and that the company, which, in point of fact, is to he the real owner of the road, should pay the interest upon the cost of these betterments plus the customs duty. My hon. friend says himself that it does not go that far. Therefore, we have it plain now that, so far as the cost of construction goes, that i-s the original cost of building the road, the customs duties will be added to the cost of construction. But -for the betterments that are made, from now to any time in the future while this road is in possession of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, importations will be made by the government and so no customs duties will be levied, but the government will import the material free of duty under the ordinary clause of the Customs Act. But, as my

bon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) lias pointed out, this is not an ordinary case. It is not a case like the Intercolonial. I quite understand that in the case of the Intercolonial, although it seems to me this clause in the Customs Act never was intended to cover that case ; yet, to a certain extent, the rule should prevail, and that everything imported, either for the construction or the improvement of the road, is regarded as imported directly by the government for its own use. But the case of the Grand Trunk Pacific is entirely different. In that case the road is leased to the company for fifty years. Practically the company becomes the owner of the road. It will he a great favour from the government to the Grand Trunk Pacific to allow the importation of material without any charge for customs duty. Now, if it is true-and I have no doubt it is-that within the next fifteen yeans the cost of construction will be doubled, we are making a very considerable present to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway in exempting them from the payment of the three per cent rental upon the customs duties upon the enormous quantity of manufactures that will be imported for betterments upon the road. And, on the other hand, it will be the greatest disadvantage to our manufacturers if this policy is carried out. I do not mean to say for a moment that the present government has adopted all our ideas on the subject of a national policy. We know very well that, although deputation after deputation has waited upon them asking for a revision of the tariff and telling them that because the tariff is not high enough a great many of our industries are suffering, up to this date the government has constantly refused to do anything to come to the relief of those industries. On the other.hand, there is no doubt that, in 1897, a certain part of the policy of the late government was adopted by lion, gentlemen opposite. They introduced at least a measure of protection to the industries of this country. Is it possible, in this great enterprise, which is going to cost so much money, and for which such immense quantities of material and supplies will be required for fifty years, they are going to strike a blow at the manufacturing industries of Canada in the way proposed ? I take it that the amendment my hop. friend (Mr. Osier) suggested to the committee the other evening should he adopted, and I would suggest to my hon. friend that he should move his amendment as an amendment to that of the hon. Minister of Justice, so as to put the policy of both parties frankly before the committee and before the country.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Casgrain) should not urge us too strougly to adopt the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, if he is really in earnest in his desire to protect our industries, because we might go the extreme limit Mr. CASGRAIN.
to which his party went in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and extend the terms of this proposal to the whole line extending to the Pacific ocean. But I do not think we shall follow that policy. The hon. gentleman said that the Act relating to the customs had not in contemplation importa-1 tions to the extent that are likely to take place under this agreement, and said that what was in contemplation was simply military clothing, musical instruments, military stores and munitions of war. But what is the provision of the Act under which all the material employed in connection with the Intercolonial comes in ? Surely the importations in connection with the Intercolonial are fully as large as they can be in connection with this enterprise. They can come in under the section my hon. friend says had not in contemplation importations of that sort.
I did not deny that.

My hon. friend must bear in mind that if we are to remedy this it is not a question of dealing with a contract, but it will be necessary to say that the government should not enjoy that exemption from the payment of duties which it has enjoyed up to the present time. My hon. friend says that, so far as this road is concerned, this is practically for the benefit of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. He must bear in mind that all this money, which is expended for the importation of materials, will remain the property of the government. Of course my friends will deny that-they appear to have denied everything, even that the sun is shining at midday-and if they read the contract, If they have not yet done so, they will see that what I say is correct, that it is merely intended to lease this road for fifty years, that at the end of that time it will revert to the government, and that all of this material- will remain the property of the government in the same way as if it were material for the Intercolonial Railway. I may add that personally I think all of "these exemptions should be abolished ; I would go in for the payment of duty with respect to the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Intercolonial Railway.
The Canadian Pacific Railway has no exemption now.
They had up to a recent date, they had after the original construction was completed.
It was limited to a very small amount, to rails and one or two supplies, rails, rail fastenings, fish plates.
And bridge material.
And material for bridges.
What is left.

Tile Minister of Justice claims that at the end of fifty years this road will belong to the government, so that it must not be loaded with heavier expenses; he forgets that the duty which should be paid in this matter will go to the government, and that therefore the government will not be loaded with any additional expense at all. What we want is that the duty should not be rebated to the Grand Trunk Pacific to the detriment of our manufacturers, that the full duty should be paid, particularly as these duties go to the government and do not in any way increase the cost to the government. In this way we would be protecting our manufacturers and that is the sole reason for introducing this clause. The very amendment which the Minister of Justice now proposes, shows that there is reason in that. Why should you enforce the payment of duty upon the first cost of this road and not upon the betterments ? Why should you, during construction, insist upon the duty being paid and the Grand Trunk Pacific paying interest on it at three per cent, although it does not cost the government anything, and then say that from the termination of the period of construction, the materials should be imported free of duty and that the three per cent should not be charged to the Grand Trunk on the amount of that duty.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) says that the contract provides that after the completion of the road, duty should not be paid on materials imported for betterments. The contract does not say that.

The contract does not say that, but the Grand Trunk will say that the government having the right to admit these things free of duty and having bound themselves to construct this road at ns low a cost as possible, having the Grand Trunk Pacific officers joint officers with the officers of the government to see that it is constructed cheaply, will be bound to admit these things free of duty. I do not see why the government do not accept the suggestion and make the amendment which the Minister of Justice has proposed to apply to the original construction, apply also to the betterments, which within fifteen or twenty years after the construction of the road will amount to as much as the original cost of construction. I do not see why he should apply the principle in one case and not in the other, having recognized that our manufacturers ought to be protected. I move that all the words after the word ' that ' in the amendment be struck out and that the following be substituted :
Provided further that notwithstanding anything contained in section 17 of the said contract all materials or supplies of any kind which are not the products of Canadian labour and which are imported for the purpose of the construction of the said eastern division by or on
behalf of the said commissioners or by or on behalf of any contractors, workmen, agents or servants for the construction of the said eastern division or for the improvement, replacement of structures or otherwise upon capital account for betterment of the said eastern division a'.s in clause 16 of the said contract provided shall be liable to the usual customs duties provided by the statutes in that behalf and should be included in and form part of the ' cost of construction ' mentioned in section 15 of the said agreement, or of the capital account or betterments mentioned in section 16 of the said agreemnt as the case may be.
I hope still that the Minister of Justice will see the importance of accepting this amendment or of adding to his own amendment words which will cover the expenditure on the capital account during the continuance of this proposed lease.

The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Osier) has stated that this road varies from a government constructed aud government-owned road, like the Intercolonial ; that there is some danger to the manufacturing industries of this country and that in future they will not have protection under the clause contained in this agreement, if the government should determine and order that certain betterments should be made upon the road and that such betterments and material for such betterments might come in free of duty. I am glad to see that my hon. friend has had his mind quieted upon another point which seemed to disconcert him a good deal. His argument in the past has been that the Grand Trunk Company would not operate this road at all ; that they would give it up, that there was no chance for their operating it, that the road would not pay and the complaint has been made that there is enough security for the government in the five million dollars of equipment.

Surely that has nothing to do with this argument; we are dealing with the contract and we must assume that it will be carried out and that the expectation of the government will he realized. We do not believe it will be realized, but at the same time we must assume that it will be, and make provision, accordingly.

Then I am correct. If the Grand Trunk Pacific do not operate it and it comes back to us it will be a government road and we will have the power to operate it; we have the power to operate it even if the terms of the lease are carried out. My hon. friend professes the greatest solicitude for the manufacturers of this country in this matter because if the government briug in materials for the betterment of this road it may injure them. The hon. gentleman assumes that some credit is due to him because the Minister of Justice introduced this resolution. The Minister of Justice tells us that it is liis judgment and the judgment of able

lawyers that this was understood and intended by the parties to this agreement, to be the meaning of the contract, but to satisfy the fears of the hon. gentlemen opposite he has introduced this amendment.
Now that this has been introduced the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) would fain claim credit, as if he had brought to the notice of the government something that had been entirely lost sight of. The hon. gentleman assured us in his statement and in the words of the resolution that he would expect that it was only to apply to the betterments of the road and only when the government ordered these betterments. This is not a question of this company bringing in these materials at their own will and pleasure and bringing them in free. If the government order this company to make betterments and this company consent and the material is brought in free, then they are not to be charged interest upon the duty that would accrue upon that. As far as the company are concerned, what does the agreement say :
The lease of the said eastern division shall contain all necessary and proper provisions required by the government for securing, during the entire term of the said lease, "the efficient maintenance and operation of the said division, including all repairs and renewals, and the maintenance and renewal of its rolling stock and equipment, so as to keep the said division, in all respects, up to the standard of modern and efficient railway practice and operation, as the same shall be advanced and improved from time to time, during the whole term of said lease, it being the intention of this agreement that the said lease shall provide, in all respects, for the upkeeping of the said eastern division and of the equipment thereof (otherwise than by expenditure upon construction account under paragraph sixteen hereof) to the satisfaction of the government, at the expense of the company, after the same shall he completed and handed over by the government to the company for operation.
The lease contains all proper provisions that this company shall maintain and keep up the road and make all renewals and repairs during the time that the lease continues. They are to make these repairs and renewals and the road is to be kept up to the standard of the efficiency of other roads as they are at that time. If a case should arise in which the government, in addition to that, shall determine that they shall have some betterment made, then we have the power to have that improvement made, and if it is made from imported material and duty is paid upon it, the interest upon that duty shall not he charged to that company. But the government cannot do this unless they have the consent of the company in doing it. If the company are bound to maintain and keep up the efficiency of the road, including renewals and repairs during all the time of the lease, I do not see that there will be very many cases where the government will ask the company to make any betterments that the company Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
under the lease are not required to make. But if they did and the company should say to them : Well, if you insist upon our doing this, we will agree to do it, we will agree to make the structures stronger than we think is necessary, but if this material has to come in from a foreign country you must not charge us interest upon the duty. That is the position, as I understand it, and I think there is very little justification for the view of the hon. gentleman who endeavours to see danger to the industrial interests of the country about which lie talks, in this provision. As far as the industrial interests are concerned, that need not be a matter of consequence. If there were to be a great expenditure in this way, if the government were voluntarily to require sometning more than the efficient maintenance and upkeeping of the road, it would not be a very grave charge upon the country. That would be the worst that would occur. The Tariff Act says that articles and goods imported for the use of the government may come in free of duty. When supplies come in for the Intercolonial Railway from foreign countries they are exempt from customs duties. Whether you approve of it or do not, that has been the law of the country for many years. I suppose it was based upon the idea tnat it would be taking the money out of one pocket and putting it in the other as far as the government is concerned. The payment is being made out of the public treasury if duties are paid the money goes back again into the public treasury. Whether it is wise or not it has been the law for many years. I do not know how far back it goes. It must have been in operation for years and years following from one tariff after another under both governments. While that has been the case, what has been the action of the government in reference to the industrial interests of the country ? In securing supplies for the Intercolonial Railway which we could have brought in free, many of the supplies have been purchased from our own manufacturers at prices higher than the government could have bought them for in foreign countries. That has been done by the government, I take it, with the approval of their followers on this side of the House, and I may say also with the approval of hon. gentlemen opposite. All the locomotives that this country could produce and sell to the Intercolonial Railway have been purchased in this country. If the government should see fit to order any betterments, of which I do not think there will be many, and the articles necessary cannot be had in this country, if your factories are so over-tcrowded with orders, as they are at the present time, that they cannot take any orders from yon, or fulfil them at the proper time, then you will go elsewhere and bring in the material, and bringing in the material, the company will not have to pay

interest on the customs duties that might or might not at that time be leviable upon (this material. Who is going to say -what the customs tariff will be in 20 or 30 years from now ? Who is going to say, under the changing conditions among all nations, what it may be ? This provision was asked for and it was conceded on the part of the government that if the government should insist upon this company making any betterments the least the government could do was to agree that if materials are imported the company should not be called upon to pay interest on the customs duties provided there are customs duties at the time when these betterments are made.
What is the object of inserting such a provision in the clause if the railway company are to keep up the road to a first-class standard ?
That is the difference between maintenance and betterment. That stipulates the kind of a road they will be bound to keep up under this lease.
And the hon. gentleman expects that it shall be kept up as a first-class road ?

Certainly. The clause says :
The lease of the said eastern division shall contain all necessary and proper provisions required by the government for securing, during the entire term of the said lease, the efficient maintenance and operation of the said division, including all repairs and renewals, and the maintenance and renewal of its rolling stock and equipment, s:o as to keep the said division, in all respects, up to the standard of modern and efficient railway practice and operation, as the same shall be advanced and improved from tdm'e to time, during the whole term of said lease, it being the intention of this agreement that the said lease shall provide, /in all respects, for the upkeeping of the said eastern division and of the equipment thereof (otherwise than by expenditure upon construction account under paragraph sixteen hereof) to the satisfaction of the government, at the expense of the company, after the same shall be completed and handed over by the government to the company for operation.
What provision does the hon. gentleman require if that contract is valid ?

My idea is that you may not require any, and therefore I say, that gentlemen opposite are getting themselves into a state of unrest and tearfulness without necessity. This lease runs for fifty years, and who can tell what may happen fifty years hence ? If this road is built up to the standard required, as it will be, hon. gentlemen must agree with me, that the government will not have to require much work to be done in the way of betterments over and above what the provisions of the lease demand. Notwithstanding what gentlemen opposite say, this is intended to be a through Canadian route, and we all hope that even if in the future it should not be able to compete with the route by rail and water, it will at least give a comparatively low rate of freight in affording an outlet for the grain shipments of the west during the winter season when lake navigation is closed. Hon. gentlemen opposite must have anticipated that a first-class high standard road would be constructed, when they put its cost at what' I consider the extravagant amount of $125,000,000. I don't suppose they think it is going to be a tramway, when they allege it will cost such a large sum. This section was introduced by the Minister of Justice,
I may say, to allay the fears of gentlemen opposite, although I have an idea that their fears are not so great as they would have us believe. I am willing to take the opinion of the Minister of Justice and the other legal gentlemen who agreed with him, that the existing clause explains fully what was meant between the parties, but if this makes it plainer, there can be no objection to it. The hon. member (Mr. Osier) thinks he is going to terrify the manufacturers of Canada by the statement that tor fifty years there may he any amount of material brought in by the government and no duty charged on it. I ask the hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. Casgraiu) if he sees any great danger to the industries of this country in that clause ? If it be the policy of future governments, as it is the policy of this government, to give a preference to Canadian manufacturers, even if a higher price be paid for them, all that enter can enter into the question would be that this company should be absolved from paying the duty on the importations of such goods as cannot he obtained here. This is a provision in the contract which looks forward to a period 50 years hence. It may be asked, why do we need to insert this clause at all, because there is no doubt that under the existing law the government can import materials free of duty. If that law continues on the statute-book, it would he sufli-cient without this clause, hut parliament can repeal that clause in the tariff Act at any time, and the company simply takes precautions here, that even if it should be repealed, th,e law in that respect shall remain as it is at present, so far as they are concerned.

The Minister of Customs has taken on a new roll just now. He has assumed the part of a lawyer, and lie is interpreting this agreement contrary to the meaning which leading lawyers give it. I have heard him in this House disclaim having any knowledge of law ; saying that he was simply a business man. He apparently has as little knowledge of railway matters as he has of law.

Let me ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) if it is.

possible for him to make any remarks in this House without trying to be personally offensive ? The hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) is not a lawyer himself. I have given my views, I think, in a manner that was not offensive to any one. Of course, I cannot control the conduct of the hon. gentleman, but I can tell him that he must not attempt to lecture me-

I would not think of such a thing.
The MINISTER OF CUSTOMS-or make himself personally offensive, because I am not disposed to submit to it, nor do 1 think it conducive to the dignity of the debate.
The Minister of Customs has told us that he is not a lawyer, and to-night lie is assuming the role of a lawyer.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) never rose yet, but he tried to insult some one.
Don't leave.
I am not going away ; don't be afraid.

The Minister of Customs apparently knows as little about railway matters as he does about law. He states, that it would be absurd to suppose that after this road has been constructed, there will be any betterments, and any additions to capital account. Now, under this contract the road when constructed will be simply a backbone ; simply two lines of rails running from one end of Canada to the other. If there is to be any such development as the government contemplates, and if the territory through which the railway runs, develops as we are told it will, then there will be sidings to be put in.
There will be branches to be put in, and a continual expenditure on capital account. If this is not the case, if this road does not, within ten or fifteen years after the backbone is constructed, require a series of roads to be sent out as ribs, it will be of no value. These roads, which will be put out as sidings and spurs here and there, are additions to the capital account of the company, and in no sense part of the working expenses. These additions, if this railway is to be a success, will come to quite the amount I am stating, that is, double the amount of the original capital within ten or fifteen years. The materials for bridges, rails and other supplies for those additions, if they come in free of duty, -will be a very serious menace to our manufacturers.
Why should they come in free of duty ?

I will tell the hon. Minister why. I was glad to hear him say that the government do not exercise their power to the fullest extent to bring in supplies free Hon. Mr. PATERSON.
of duty for the Intercolonial Railway. But I will tell him why these should come in free of duty. There is an agreement that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company shall pay interest only on the net cost of this road. The net cost is the lowest cost at which the materials can be had in the lowest markets of the world. That is my contention, backed up by legal opinions. I am afraid that the minister must feel that his cause is weak.
It was only the Minister of Justice saying that there was no such thing in the contract, that is all.

I cannot make the minister agree with that interpretation of the clause. The government, in dealing witii the Intercolonial Railway, have the right to admit materials free of duty or to pay duty. When they are dealing with the Grand Trunk Pacific, they have made a contract that they are not to charge that company interest except on the lowest cost of the materials wherever they can be got. That Is a very serious difference between the two cases, and it is one reason why the provision kliould now be made that duty should be charged and interest paid upon it. The hon. Minister of Customs says that during the long period of the lease the customs duties may be changed or they may be abolished altogether. Some of us on this side of the House hope they will be increased. But that is all the more reason why we should understand now' that duties will be charged against the Grand Trunk Pacific on whatever materials may be used for the betterment of the road, and will be added to capital. I think the interpretation which I have put upon that is the correct one. If the hon. Minister of Customs will W'ork it out, he will see that I am correct. I am very sorry indeed if any words I said were applied personally to the hon. Minister of Customs. I would not have him think I intended it for a moment.
I would not if it were not your usual liabiit.

I am sorry if I have offended the hon. minister. I would not willingly offend him in any way, for there is no member of the government for whom I have a higher respect than the hon. Minister of Customs.
Mr. CAiSGRAIN. I hope I shall not have the misfortune of making my hon. friend the Minister of Customs angry ; but I want to show the difference between clause 23 and clause 16 of the agreement. I do not know whether the same distinction exists in the English law that exists in the French law\ In the French law there are certain repairs and renewals w'hich the lessee is ob-iged to make ; and certain repairs which the lessor is oblige to make, the same distinction seems to be carried out in this

contract. The repairs, renewals and maintenance of the road, andi the maintenance and renewal of the rolling stock and equipment as defined in clause 23, are the ordinary renewals and repairs which the lessee is to make. This clause by the parenthesis ' otherwise than by expenditure upon construction under paragraph sixteen thereof,' refers us back to clause 16, which applies to a different kind of repairs, renewals and maintenance altogether. It refers to betterments chargeable to capital account. So that I take it that under this agreement if the government wishes to 'better this road, to improve it up to the standard for the time being, or to introduce into it more modern structures, upon the materials for that work no duty will be charged, because that will be done by the government themselves. Then we have simply the promise in section 23 that the lease shall contain these stipulations. When the government and the company come together to execute this lease, we do not know whether or not the promise which is made to the committee this evening will be carried out. In the event of any betterment or improvement being required by the necessities'of the time, we do not know whether or not the company will not say to the government, it is your bounden duty and obligation under this agreement to make these betterments and renewals yourselves. If I am correct in the interpretation I give to this contract, all these betterments and improvements which in the course of time will have to be made to the railway, will be made by the government, and not by the company, and therefore the government will import these materials itself and not pay any duty on them. It is the same difference between the parties that has always existed. We wish our manufacturers to be protected as much as possible. If this road is to be renewed in the manner stipulated in paragraph 16, if materials are to be imported, our manufacturers should be protected against importations coming from the United States, Germany, Belgium or any other country. It is not fair to our manufacturers that these materials should be importel to their detriment and disadvantage. Something has been said about the ownership of the road and the termination of the lease,
Under this agreement the lease was to be made for fifty years. But paragraph 21 goes further and says :
If, upon the termination of the said lease, the government shall determine not to undertake the operation of the said eastern division, the company, provided the terms offered by it are as favourable to the government as those offered by any other railway company equally competent to perform and fulfil the obligations required by the government to be assumed by the lessees thereof, shall have the right to an extension or renewal of the said lease for a further period of fifty years, upon such terms as may be agreed upon. Notices of the intention of the parties shall be given as may in such lease be provided.
Now, it seems to me, this is practically a lease to that Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for one hundred years. For, after that company has operated this railway for fifty years, it is not at all probable that any other company will step in and offer tlie government better terms than can be offered by the company that has had the railway under its control for so long a time. This is a different case from that of the Intercolonial. The Intercolonial belongs to the government, and by stretching-I say it advisedly, by stretching-the terms of the Customs Act, anything imported for the railway is held to be imported for tlie government. But in tlie case of tlie Grand Trunk Pacific anything imported is imported for the Grand Trunk Pacific, and not for the government.

I confess that I am unable to understand the interpretation the Minister of Customs gives to that portion of the contract under which the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company is bound to keep the road as it receives tlie road, in first-class condition. I made a five minutes speech in 1882-the only political speech I ever made in my life up to 1896- in support of my kinsman, the Minister of Militia. In that speech I made no reference to the national policy or to the trade policy. I am inconsistent to that extent, if my hon. friend regards it as inconsistent, but I am not ashamed of having made that speech or supported that gentleman. Probably if I were not so actively engaged in public life, personal considerations might induce me to support him again. I would not be ashamed to do so, but I do not want my hon. friend to understand on that account that I am guilty of one-hundredth part of the inconsistencies of which he stands convicted in this House to-day. Did he or did he not in Nova Scotia himself move a resolution against the duties on foodstuffs, denouncing those duties as having been created in the interests of the Ontario mil-

lers, and calling on the Dominion government to repeal them? And has he not, In the last seven years, been acting as Finance Minister without taking a step to carry out the resolution he then proposed ? Which does he regard as a greater inconsistency-that five minutes speech of which I am not ashamed, or his own attitude as a minister of the Crown, faced with his own resolution in the Nova Scotia legislature calling these duties odious and hateful, and yet remaining seven years a minister of the Crown of Canada and permitting these very duties to continue to be inflicted on the people of his province ? Is he or is he not the same gentleman who advocated in Nova Scotia-advocated because he was forced to do so, and hot because he believed in it-the secession of all the maritime provinces from the Dominion ? And this is the gentleman who is lecturing me about inconsistency.
No, the lecture began on that side.

Is he or is he not the same gentleman who in Nova Scotia, on more than one platform, denounced the duties on coal and iron and told the people they had better give their attention to agriculture and fishing ? And is he not the same gentleman who during this very session submitted a resolution in this parliament to encourage these very industries of coal and iron ? Is he or is he not the same gentleman who went through the province of Nova Scotia and denounced on every public platform the alleged extravagance of the Conservative administration of this Dominion, and who has since made a record of himself as a spendthrift Minister of Finance ? Is he not the same gentleman who went through Nova Scotia denouncing protection in every shape and form, and who now, as Finance Minister, has a tariff in force which his own friends are commending as a protective tariff to the manufacturers of Canada ? Does the hon. gentleman charge me with inconsistency ? Is there not something said somewhere about the man who desired to pull the mote out of his neighbour's eye and had no regard for the beam in his own ? I do not want to discuss these old issues, and only refer to them because of some sneering observations which the hon. gentleman made in reply to myself concerning the patriotism of hon. gentlemen on this side. We know, with regard to Canadian patriotism, what is the hon. gentleman's record.
I did not introduce this discussion, but if the hon. gentleman desires a discussion of this kind, there is no reason why he should not be accommodated on any occasion.

I must correct my hon. friend when he says that I made -some sneering allusion to the patriotism of hon. gentlemen opposite. I am in the judgment of the House when I say that 3S2
I made no such allusion. So far as there has been any calling into question the consistency or patriotism of any hon. gentleman, it is my hon. friend who is in fault, and he must hold himself and not me responsible for any disagreeable consequences. With regard to the five minute speech, I take it for granted that my hon. friend does not mean to say that that was the ouly identification he had with the Liberal party. He was a member of the Liberal party, counted as such, belonging to a well-known Liberal family, and everybody in Nova SCotia looked upon him as a pronounced Liberal. Whether he made a speech of five minutes or five hours does not alter the fact that he appeared on the public platform as a champion of the Liberal candidate, opposed to the Dominion government. With regard to the question of confederation, which the hon. gentleman has brought up, I have never been ashamed of my attitude in that regard. I am not ashamed of the fact that I was an anti-confederate in the province of Nova Scotia, nor of my record on that question. No doubt many gentlemen who hear me now and who are great federationists, if they had lived in Nova Scotia in those days would have been anticonfederates. The great mass of the people, and especially the more influential classes, were anti-confederates. In fact the Conservative party would have perished years ago if they had not brought anti-confederate blood into their rank-s to help them. The hon. gentleman is not the first who joined the Conservative party. The Hon. Joseph Howe, perhaps the greatest man Nova Scotia ever produced, was an anti-confederate, but the Conservative party brought him into their ranks and made him a cabinet minister. The Hon. A. W. McLelan was an anti-confederate whom they brought into their ranks and made a cabinet minister. Sir John Thompson was an anti-confederate, and they brought him into their ranks and made him a cabinet minister, and a great one he was. If the Conservative party had been confined to their old blood, they would have perished years ago, and they were only kept alive by calling in from time to time, good, sound specimens of anti-confederate blood, some of whom I have mentioned.

I think at least my hon. friend has confessed one thing, and that is that the very best men that ever were in the anti-confederate party of Nova Scotia long since left it and joined the Conservative party.

That may be so, yet it is an established fact that if the present men who come from Nova Scotia are not up to ttye high standard the hon. gentleman would establish, they have the good fortune to command in a larger degree than he and his friends were ever able, the confidence of a people who are not behind those of any province in the appreciation of public affairs.

As far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned, I want to remind my hon. friend that, as far back as 1887, it gave a very substantial majority to the late Sir John Macdonald's administration, and in support of the national policy of which he was the founder and creator-a policy which recommended itself to the province of Nova Scotia in spite of all the efforts of my hon. friend and his associates to discredit it in the minds of the people and make them believe, by sectional appeals, that it was conceived altogether in the interests of the upper provinces.

And for long years before that and long years afterward the people of Nova Scotia were good enough to set the seal of their confidence and approval on their humble servant who now addresses the House, and when he closed his career as Prime Minister of that province and came to Ottawa to take,part in that larger arena, they continue their confidence by sending him here with an increased majority.
Which is likely to entirely disappear at the next election.
Let me remind my hon. friend that he is not the first Nova Scotian sitting in that seat who made just the same prediction.
And many of whose predictions, particularly with regard to the west, are only beginning to be realized by my hon. friends on the other side.
My hon. friend may do well to appeal to the great west where they do not know either of us so well as do the people of Nova Scotia. I confined myself to the question of Nova Scotia.

If my hon. friend goes to the great west, he may as well repeat there the statements made by him in the province of Nova Scotia that the construction of railways is more needful to us than to the great provinces of the west, because the great provinces of the west are not needful to confederation.

I am not going to refer to that Nova Scotian part of that question, but only to allude to one remark made by the leader of the opposition. He says that the government have not done much in the way of securing Canadian routes for the traffic of the Northwest but are depending upon the patriotism of the people there. I wish to point out that the government have made a contract with this company under which, unless a Canadian deliberately goes and asks specifically to have his stuff sent to American ports, it will go through Canadian ports by virtue of the contract.	*
Amendment (Mr. Barkex-) negatived.
